Among the authors of compendia on Smṛti, Hemādri is indeed generally regarded as preeminent.

He indeed adorned the office of chief minister to Mahādeva, the great emperor (mahārāja-cakravartin) and son of Caitrapāladeva, the ruler of the Devagiri region; and this Mahādeva [ascended] the lion-throne of the kingdom of Devagiri in the year one thousand eighty-one of the Śaka era.
"He descended into intoxication"— such is the declaration of those who know the ancient truths.

Indeed, by that very Hemādri, the authority of the *Smṛtinibandha* named *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, which was composed by him, has been established by all later scholars, such as Raghunandana Bhaṭṭācārya.
This has been accepted without contradiction by the authors of Smṛti commentaries, beginning with Ācārya.

Due to the bulk of the work and the great abundance of necessary subjects to be established, these statements— extracted from the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other sources whose authority is beyond doubt— are presented here.

Furthermore, because this *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* abounds [in its contents], it is clearly evident to all connoisseurs of the compendia of Smṛti that its name is entirely true to its meaning (*anvarthanāman*).
It achieves the propagation and advancement of the various essential branches of learning belonging to both the East and the West.

The world-renowned institution named the "Asiatic Society," which possesses a well-established foundation, whose web of fame serves as its very ornament, and which enjoys the highest honor, has risen like the entire orb of the sun.
Having obtained the command of the renowned assembly of learned men, I have resolved to publish this single section of that very *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, known as the *Prāyaścittakhaṇḍa*.
(100) Indeed, with great reverence, I have undertaken this great undertaking for ten years.
As long as the process of printing this work was being carried out by me,
it has now reached completion. For the preparation and printing of this work, three manuscript copies were [utilized].
These books have been acquired by me and examined according to my understanding. Among them, one was purchased from Kāśī on behalf of the Asiatic Society,
and the second was obtained from Kāśī through the kindness of the honorable Bālamukunda Mālavīya.

I have acquired a third manuscript; having relied upon one manuscript obtained from Vārāṇasī itself, it was transcribed for the President of the Asiatic Society. Among these three manuscripts, the one acquired through the kindness of Mālavimahodaya—
Setting aside two manuscripts that were heavily corrupted with errors and contained passages that were frequently disjointed,
[I have relied on] those published by the renowned scholarly society known as the Asiatic Society.
This section of the work consisting of the Prāyaścitta-khaṇḍa appears to be entirely distinct from the other portions of the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi.
This distinction is so very clear that by examining it, the Caturvarga—

A great doubt has indeed arisen in my mind, increasing further and further, as to whether or not there exists a portion consisting of the Prāyaścitta-khaṇḍa for the illustrious Hemādri— who is world-renowned as the creator of the Cintāmaṇi and who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the meaning of all the Dharmaśāstras.
Indeed, he proceeds by way of acceptance.
For instance, in all authoritative compendia of Smṛti, those specific expiations which have been established for particular sins through various scriptural statements are now [being] presented.
(10) They are indeed found in this section on penance (*prāyaścitta-khaṇḍa*), for the most part, in relation to those very same sins.

Penances contrary to those [faults] are seen to be established by very different scriptural statements. Furthermore, regarding the great sins known as killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, violating the teacher’s wife, and association with those [who have committed such acts]— [The text continues: ...in these cases, penances are observed to be prescribed by various authorities according to differences in intention, repetition, and so forth. Moreover, it is seen that for some of these, there are penances that lead to purification even while one remains in the state of an outcaste (*patita*), whereas for others, there are none. Therefore, because of this diversity of scriptural injunctions, the determination of the appropriate penance must be made through the consideration of the specific circumstances. Thus, the penances for killing a Brahmin are established by various authorities: by Manu, by Yama, by Śātātapa, by Āpastamba, and by others. Among them, some prescribe penances that result in purification while one remains an outcaste, while others do not. For instance, the following is stated by Manu: "A Brahmin who has intentionally killed a Brahmin shall live for twelve years, performing the *Prājāpatya* penance, carrying a skull and a staff, proclaiming his deed, and dwelling outside the village. And elsewhere: "Having killed a Brahmin, one shall live for twelve years in the forest, subsisting on alms, wearing matted hair, and carrying a staff and a skull. Furthermore, those statements from the Saṃhitās and Purāṇas which establish expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) for sins,
and which have been cited with a single consensus by all other authors of digests (nibandha), have for the most part been utterly neglected in this work.
There is a great difference in magnitude.
In the portions of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* other than this specific work— namely, those sections that treat subjects such as conduct (*ācāra*), sacraments (*saṃskāra*), and gifts (*dāna*)—
there is no such [conciseness] regarding the presentation of their respective meanings.

A distinction from other compendia (*smṛtinibandha*) is generally observed; for instance, in the various specific sections of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* that expound upon conduct (*ācāra*) and so forth, one can see exactly by which statements those matters of conduct and the like were set forth, and in what manner, as compared with other compendia.

Furthermore, even though there are occasional differences regarding certain defects, it has been observed with great precision that, for the most part, those very same practices and so forth have been set forth by those very words in exactly that manner.
Furthermore, regarding those statements extracted from the Dharma-saṃhitās composed by Manu and other great sages which are established within this section on expiation (prāyaścitta):
This is a great marvel: that those statements are generally not found now in the Saṃhitā texts composed by the great sages such as Manu, whether they be printed or in manuscript form;
nevertheless, some such statements [are provided] here to produce conviction in the hearts of the discerning.
Examples are cited as follows:

In this work, on page 13, in the section concerning the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*): "For [killing] a cow, one should give two hundred; for killing a twice-born man, one thousand; then the king should fine an old woman two hundred, [and she should go to] the cow-pen."
This statement of Manu was cited on the grounds that its meaning was extremely obscure; however,
having searched systematically through both printed and manuscript editions of the Manusmṛti,
I have not found this verse therein— this is a matter of great significance.
The cause for doubt regarding the authority of this work is as follows,
on page 586 of this book:
Listen, O Dhammañja, I shall speak once more of the cow that yields all desires as gold;
the twice-born who accepts it becomes an outcast immediately.
O King, the atonement for that very [sin] occurs again through the instruction of Brahmā;
O King, it is achieved by reciting [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times, or else by expending one-eighth of one's wealth.
"Or by consecration, O Śambhu, or by sacrifices with all their ritual fees—
by these one attains purity, which is beneficial for both worlds.
These three verses and many others of this kind belong to the *Mahābhārata*.

Having done so, these [verses] were extracted and found here; however, while searching with great effort through modern printed editions of the Mahābhārata, not a single one of these verses was found by me.

In this very manner, those statements from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, *Matsya Purāṇa*, *Liṅga Purāṇa*, *Padma Purāṇa*, and others which have been cited in this work are generally not found within the printed or manuscript editions of those respective Purāṇas.
Such characteristics as these serve as grounds for doubting the authority of this work.
Having extensively observed many great differences between this work and other treatises on the Smṛtis, as well as other sections of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, this book [is] the *Caturvarga-*...
Whether this was indeed composed by Hemādri, whose fame is celebrated as a maker of wish-fulfilling gems, or whether it is something new— this is truly a great doubt in my mind;
as for whether it is actually sound or not, let those of sharp intellect, who have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), determine it.
"May the learned and connoisseurs examine this," he thus humbly and respectfully submits to them—
Tarkabhūṣaṇopādhyāya.
Śrī Pramathanātha Śarmā, Professor of the Dharma-Mīmāṃsā Śāstra at the Calcutta Government Sanskrit College.

Translated into Japanese by Ken Sakurabe and Nobuchiyo Otani, *Kusharon no Genten Kaimei: Honjibun 4–20* (Clarification of the Original Text of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya: Chapters 4–20), Hōzōkan, 1999, pp. 325–368. (The following is a translation of the section concerning the ten fetters [saṃyojana] from p. 330 onwards. Regarding the statement that "the ten fetters are taught in the Sūtra," the ten fetters are as follows: the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and the five higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). Among these, the five lower fetters are: 1. the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), 2. the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), 3. the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), 4. the fetter of grasping at precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*), and 5. the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*). The five higher fetters are: 6. the fetter of desire for existence (*bhavarāga-saṃyojana*), 7. the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), 8. the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), 9. the fetter of restlessness (*auddhatya-saṃyojana*), and 10. the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*). Among these, the fetter of attachment is the greed (*lobha*) belonging to the three realms. The fetter of aversion is the hatred (*dveṣa*) belonging to the Desire Realm. The fetter of views consists of the five views: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the view of grasping at precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). The fetter of grasping at precepts and vows is the view that regards precepts, vows, or ascetic practices as the supreme means for attaining purification or liberation; it is a specific type of view. The fetter of doubt is the uncertainty regarding the Truths. The fetter of desire for existence is the greed belonging to the Form and Formless Realms. The fetter of pride is the seven types of pride (*māna*) and the like. The fetter of ignorance is the lack of knowledge regarding the Truths. The fetter of restlessness is the agitation of the mind. The fetter of envy is the resentment toward the prosperity of others. Furthermore, among these ten fetters, eight are abandoned through Seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) and two are abandoned through Meditation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). Specifically, the fetters of views, doubt, and the fetter of grasping at precepts and vows are abandoned through Seeing. The remaining seven fetters are abandoned through Meditation. Moreover, the fetters of attachment, aversion, and ignorance are abandoned through both Seeing and Meditation. The fetters of pride and restlessness are abandoned only through Meditation. The fetter of envy is abandoned only through Meditation. Regarding the distinction between the fetters of views and the fetter of grasping at precepts and vows: while the former refers to the five views themselves, the latter refers to the view that considers those very views, or precepts and vows, to be the supreme means for attaining purification or liberation. It is because this view obstructs the path to Nirvana that it is established as a separate fetter. Furthermore, although the fetter of doubt is not a defiled state of mind itself, it is included among the fetters because it gives rise to the various afflictions. Regarding the distinction between the fetters of attachment and the fetter of desire for existence: both are forms of greed, but the former refers to greed belonging to the Desire Realm, whereas the latter refers to greed belonging to the Form and Formless Realms. Regarding the fetter of pride: although it is a form of delusion, it is established as a separate fetter because it is a distinct mental factor that causes the mind to become haughty and arrogant. Regarding the fetter of restlessness: although it is a form of greed, it is established as a separate fetter because it is a distinct mental factor that agitates the mind and prevents tranquility. Regarding the fetter of envy: although it is a form of hatred, it is established as a separate fetter because it is a distinct mental factor that specifically resents the prosperity of others. Thus, the ten fetters are taught in the Sūtra as the bonds that bind sentient beings to the cycle of birth and death. By severing these fetters, one attains liberation. Therefore, one should strive to abandon them through the practice of the Path. (Note: This translation is based on the Japanese translation by Ken Sakurabe and Nobuchiyo Otani, *Kusharon no Genten Kaimei: Honjibun 4–20*, Hōzōkan, 1999, pp. 330–335.)

What, monks, is the person who is like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, his friends, his relatives, and his kinsmen; he dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his village, his town, his city, his country, and his kingdom. [Page 442–442] [Page 443–443] [Page 444–444] [Page 442–442] Furthermore, if one asks how it is that the *dharmadhātu* is not perceived by the *ālayavijñāna*, it is because the *dharmadhātu* is the object of the *manovijñāna*. Since the *ālayavijñāna* does not take the *dharmadhātu* as its object, it does not perceive it. Moreover, the *ālayavijñāna* is always associated with the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*), whereas the *manovijñāna* is associated with the five specific mental factors (*paricchedaka-caitta*). Because the *manovijñāna* possesses these specific mental factors, it perceives the *dharmadhātu*; since the *ālayavijñāna* lacks them, it does not. Furthermore, the *ālayavijñāna* is always accompanied by the four afflictions (*kleśa*)—namely, self-view, self-pride, self-love, and ignorance—which obscure the true nature of reality; therefore, it does not perceive the *dharmadhātu*. The *manovijñāna*, however, is not necessarily accompanied by these afflictions, and thus it can perceive the *dharmadhātu*. Also, the *ālayavijñāna* is always accompanied by the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), which is incapable of discerning the characteristics of objects; therefore, it does not perceive the *dharmadhātu*. The *manovijñāna*, on the other hand, is associated with all three types of feeling and is capable of discerning the characteristics of objects, and thus it perceives the *dharmadhātu*. For these reasons, the *dharmadhātu* is not perceived by the *ālayavijñāna*. [Page 443–443] Regarding the statement that the *ālayavijñāna* is "not manifest" (*apratyakṣa*), this means that it is not directly perceived by the six consciousnesses. It is like the fact that the *ālayavijñāna* itself is not perceived by the *ālayavijñāna*. Furthermore, the *ālayavijñāna* is not manifest because it is subtle and difficult to know, and because it is obscured by the four afflictions such as self-view. It is like the fact that the *ālayavijñāna* is not perceived by the *manovijñāna*. Also, the *ālayavijñāna* is not manifest because it is always accompanied by the feeling of equanimity, which is incapable of discerning the characteristics of objects. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Śubhavyūha. He had a son named Śrīcandra, who was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by all. When the prince reached maturity, he took a wife from a noble family. After some time, she conceived a child. When the pregnancy reached its full term, the queen gave birth to a son. His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, and his radiance surpassed that of a thousand suns. At the moment of his birth, the earth trembled in six ways, and a great light illuminated the entire world. Because of this, the king and his ministers named him Mahāprabha. As the boy grew, he became skilled in all arts and sciences. One day, while traveling through the city, he saw a group of elderly people, their bodies bent and their hair white, walking with difficulty. Seeing them, he asked his charioteer: ‘Why do these people have such deformed bodies? The charioteer replied: ‘This is the nature of old age; it is the law of the world. Mahāprabha then asked again: ‘Is this condition limited to these few, or will it come to me as well? The charioteer answered: ‘It will come to you too, O Prince. Hearing this, the prince was deeply distressed and returned to the palace in sorrow. Later, he encountered a group of sick people, their bodies emaciated and suffering from various ailments. Upon seeing them, he asked his charioteer: ‘What is wrong with these people? The charioteer replied: ‘This is the nature of sickness; it afflicts all living beings. Mahāprabha asked again: ‘Is this sickness limited to these few, or will it come to me as well? The charioteer answered: ‘It will come to you too, O Prince. Hearing this, the prince was overcome with grief and returned to the palace. Subsequently, he saw a group of dead people, their bodies lying on the ground, surrounded by mourners weeping and wailing.

Seeing this, he asked his charioteer: ‘Why are these people lying here? The charioteer replied: ‘This is death; it is the end of life for all. Mahāprabha asked again: ‘Is this death limited to these few, or will it come to me as well? The charioteer answered: ‘It will come to you too, O Prince. Hearing this, the prince was filled with profound anxiety and resolved to seek the path of liberation. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “At that time, King Śubhavyūha’s son Mahāprabha was none other than myself. Because I encountered these four sights—old age, sickness, death, and the renunciation of worldly life—I developed a mind of detachment and sought the supreme enlightenment. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should know that the Dharma of impermanence is the most urgent matter; you must strive diligently to transcend the cycle of birth and death. The Buddha further said: “In the past, there was a king named Brahmadatta. He had a son named Candraprabha, who was wise and compassionate. One day, the prince went out to the pleasure gardens and saw an ascetic practicing austerities in the forest. Seeing his serene countenance and disciplined conduct, the prince approached him and asked: ‘Why do you live in this wilderness, enduring such hardships? The ascetic replied: ‘I seek to escape the suffering of saṃsāra and attain the peace of nirvāṇa. Candraprabha was deeply moved by these words and immediately abandoned his royal pleasures to follow the ascetic. Through diligent practice, he mastered all meditative concentrations and attained the state of an arhat. Thus, bhikṣus, you should know that even those who possess great power and wealth must eventually renounce them to seek the true Dharma. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Mahāratha. He had a daughter named Ratnaprabhā, who was beautiful and virtuous. One day, a sage named Jyotirasa came to the palace and prophesied: ‘This princess will give birth to a son who will become a universal monarch, ruling over the four continents. Hearing this, the king rejoiced greatly. However, when the princess reached marriageable age, she refused to accept any suitor. She said: ‘I wish to remain celibate and seek the path of liberation. The king, though concerned, respected her resolve and allowed her to live in seclusion. Later, she gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of a great man. Because of the prophecy, they named him Cakravartin. As the prince grew, he became skilled in all martial arts and governance. One day, he saw an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a wandering mendicant. Stricken by the realization of the suffering of the world, he renounced his kingdom and became a śramaṇa. Through his practice, he attained the fruit of arhatship. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should know that the pursuit of the Dharma transcends all worldly attachments. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Vimalaprabha. He had a son named Sūryaprabha, who was brave and wise. One day, the prince went hunting in the mountains and encountered a starving tigress about to devour her cubs. Moved by compassion, he offered his own body to the tigress so that she might save her young. Seeing this act of self-sacrifice, the gods rained down flowers and praised him, saying: ‘This prince possesses a heart of great compassion; he will surely attain supreme enlightenment. Because of this deed, Sūryaprabha was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he served the Bodhisattva Maitreya. Thus, bhikṣus, you should know that the practice of compassion is the root of all merit. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Śuddhodana. He had a son named Siddhārtha, who was destined to become a buddha. One day, while traveling in the city, he saw the four signs of old age, sickness, death, and renunciation. Deeply affected by the suffering of the world, he left the palace at night and went forth into homelessness. Under the guidance of Ārāḍa Kālāma and Udraka Rāmaputra, he practiced various ascetic disciplines. However, realizing that these paths did not lead to liberation, he sat beneath the Bodhi tree and defeated the hosts of Māra. On the morning of the seventh week, he attained perfect enlightenment and became the Buddha Śākyamuni. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should know that the path to buddhahood requires the abandonment of all worldly desires and the cultivation of wisdom and compassion. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Aśoka. He ruled over Jambudvīpa with justice and kindness. One day, he heard of the appearance of a buddha in the world and traveled to the place where the Buddha was teaching. Upon seeing the Buddha’s majestic form and hearing his sublime Dharma, the king was filled with joy and faith. He requested ordination and became a bhikṣu. Through diligent study and meditation, he attained the fruit of arhatship. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should know that meeting a buddha and receiving the Dharma is a rare opportunity that should not be missed. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Bimbisāra. He had a son named Ajātaśatru, who later imprisoned his father and plotted against the Buddha. However, the Buddha, out of great compassion, taught him the Dharma, leading him to repent and seek refuge. Ajātaśatru then visited the Buddha frequently and offered great offerings. Because of this, he was able to alleviate his karmic obstacles and attain rebirth in a pure land. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should know that even those who have committed grave offenses can find purification through sincere repentance and devotion to the Buddha. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Prasenajit. He was a devoted follower of the Buddha and often provided for the Sangha. One day, a famine occurred in the kingdom, and the people suffered greatly. The king, wishing to relieve the distress of his subjects, made a vow to offer his own body as food to the starving. The gods, knowing his intention, sent down rain, ending the famine. Because of this act of selflessness, the king’s merit increased, and he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should know that the practice of generosity is the foundation of all virtues. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Mahāsudarś

[page 484-to-484] [page 485-to-485] [page 486-to-486] The Blessed One said this: “Ānanda, there are these four supports for the mind. What four? They are: the support for the mind that is the basis of joy; the support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity; the support for the mind that is the basis of compassion; and the support for the mind that is the basis of loving-kindness. These, Ānanda, are the four supports for the mind. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four ways of abiding. What four? They are: the way of abiding in which one dwells with oneself as an island and with oneself as a refuge; the way of abiding in which one dwells with the Dharma as an island and with the Dharma as a refuge; the way of abiding in which one dwells with no other island and no other refuge; and the way of abiding in which one dwells having transcended both the perception of form and the perception of the formless, with the cessation of perception and feeling, attaining the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These, Ānanda, are the four ways of abiding. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four fruits of the ascetic life. What four? They are: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. These, Ānanda, are the four fruits of the ascetic life. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four noble lineages. What four? They are: the noble lineage of contentment with any kind of robe, the noble lineage of contentment with any kind of almsfood, the noble lineage of contentment with any kind of lodging, and the noble lineage of delight in solitude. These, Ānanda, are the four noble lineages. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four bases of psychic power. What four? They are: the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by effort of will; the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy accompanied by effort of will; the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by effort of will; and the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by effort of will. These, Ānanda, are the four bases of psychic power. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four analytical knowledges. What four? They are: analytical knowledge of meaning, analytical knowledge of phenomena, analytical knowledge of language, and analytical knowledge of eloquence. These, Ānanda, are the four analytical knowledges. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. What four? They are: the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena. These, Ānanda, are the four foundations of mindfulness. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four right endeavors. What four? They are: the right endeavor to prevent the arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; the right endeavor to abandon arisen evil, unwholesome states; the right endeavor to produce unarisen wholesome states; and the right endeavor to maintain and perfect arisen wholesome states. These, Ānanda, are the four right endeavors. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four bases of power. What four? They are: the base of power that is concentration of desire accompanied by effort of will; the base of power that is concentration of energy accompanied by effort of will; the base of power that is concentration of mind accompanied by effort of will; and the base of power that is concentration of investigation accompanied by effort of will. These, Ānanda, are the four bases of power. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four noble truths. What four? They are: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These, Ānanda, are the four noble truths. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four fruits of the homeless life. What four? They are: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. These, Ānanda, are the four fruits of the homeless life. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower growing in mud but not soiled by it; the person who is like a white lotus flower growing in mud but even more pure than the former; the person who is like a red lotus flower growing in mud but even more radiant than the former; and the person who is like a blue lotus flower growing in mud but even more fragrant than the former. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four ways of entering the womb. What four? They are: entering the womb with full awareness and remaining with full awareness; entering the womb with full awareness but remaining without full awareness; entering the womb without full awareness but remaining with full awareness; and entering the womb without full awareness and remaining without full awareness. These, Ānanda, are the four ways of entering the womb. “Furthermore, Ānanda, there are these four kinds of assemblies. What four? [Page 511–513] Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, does not become afraid, nor terrified, nor fall into terror, then this should be known as the sign that he will not regress from full enlightenment. Moreover, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, reflects thus: "This is the path of the Tathāgatas; this is the path by which the Tathāgatas have attained manifestly perfect enlightenment," and if, so reflecting, his mind does not waver and he does not lose heart, then this should be known as the sign that he will not regress from full enlightenment. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a person were to see the tracks of a great elephant in the forest. Seeing them, he would know with certainty: "A great elephant has passed here. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this profound perfection of wisdom and does not become afraid, nor terrified, nor fall into terror, one should know with certainty: "This bodhisattva mahāsattva has come from afar; he has practiced the bodhisattva path for a long time; he has served many Buddhas; he has planted roots of merit under many Buddhas; he has been predicted by the Tathāgatas; he is not led astray by others; he is protected by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a woman were pregnant. If she does not walk about much, does not exert herself, does not eat unwholesome food, and avoids all things that cause distress, one would know with certainty: "This woman will give birth to a boy; she will not give birth to a girl. Why is that? Because such are the signs of a woman who is carrying a boy. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this profound perfection of wisdom and does not become afraid, nor terrified, nor fall into terror, one should know with certainty: "This bodhisattva mahāsattva will go forth to full enlightenment; he will not turn back from it. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a king were to have a son born to him. As soon as he is born, he is anointed as the heir apparent. Even though he is a child, because of his anointment, he is superior to all the ministers. In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva may be a beginner, if he hears this profound perfection of wisdom and does not become afraid, nor terrified, nor fall into terror, he is nevertheless superior to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the giver of light, and the producer of the Tathāgatas. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a master thief were to enter a house by means of a hole and then escape through another hole. Those who catch him would say: "This man has entered by one hole and escaped by another. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the door of the Dharma-realm by means of the perfection of wisdom and then departs by means of skillful means, those who follow him should know: "This bodhisattva mahāsattva has entered the door of the Dharma-realm by means of the perfection of wisdom and has departed by means of skillful means. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a great cloud were to arise over the world-system, bringing rain upon all grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees according to their capacity. Some grasses, shrubs, and herbs would absorb a small amount of water; some would absorb a medium amount; and some would absorb a large amount. Yet the great cloud does not think: "I am giving water to these various beings according to their capacity. Nevertheless, each receives according to its own nature. In the same way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, having arisen in the world, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings through the single vehicle, the Buddha-vehicle. He does not think: "I am teaching the Dharma to these various beings according to their faculties. Nevertheless, each sentient being receives the Dharma according to their own capacity. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a skilled physician were to prepare a medicine for all diseases. If there were a person suffering from a disease who took that medicine, they would be cured of their illness. In the same way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata prepares the medicine of the Dharma for all the afflictions of sentient beings. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes up this profound perfection of wisdom, he will be cured of all the afflictions of ignorance and will attain manifestly perfect enlightenment. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to reach the further shore of all dharmas should train in this profound perfection of wisdom. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to transcend the world with its gods, humans, and asuras should train in this profound perfection of wisdom. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to lead all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa should train in this profound perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, rejoices and exults, one should know that he is near to full enlightenment. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, feels a sense of urgency and thinks: "How wonderful that I have encountered this profound perfection of wisdom! then he should be known as one who is irreversible from full enlightenment. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a merchant leader were to set out on a journey to a great ocean. Before setting out, he would examine the marks of the great ocean. Having examined them, he would know with certainty: "The great ocean is not far off. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this profound perfection of wisdom and feels a sense of urgency, one should know with certainty: "This bodhisattva mahāsattva is not far from manifestly perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a person were to dream that they were traveling toward the great ocean. Upon waking, they would remember that dream. One should know that this person is not far from the great ocean. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dreams that they hear this profound perfection of wisdom being taught, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is not far from manifestly perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a person were to see the tracks of a caravan leader in the wilderness. Seeing them, they would know with certainty: "A great caravan leader has passed here. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the tracks of this profound perfection of wisdom, one should know with certainty: "A great caravan leader of the Dharma has passed here. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a person were to see the smoke rising from a great city.

Seeing it, they would know with certainty: "A great city is not far off. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the smoke of this profound perfection of wisdom, one should know with certainty: "The great city of the Dharma is not far off. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a person were to see the banners of a great king. Seeing them, they would know with certainty: "A great king is not far off. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the banners of this profound perfection of wisdom, one should know with certainty: "The great King of the Dharma is not far off. Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a person were to see the rising sun. Seeing it, they would know with certainty: "The sun is not far off. In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the rising of this profound perfection of wisdom, one should know with certainty: "The light of the Tathāgata is not far off. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to see the Buddhas and Blessed Ones of the ten directions should train in this profound perfection of wisdom. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to hear the Dharma from those Buddhas and Blessed Ones should train in this profound perfection of wisdom. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to serve those Buddhas and Blessed Ones should train in this profound perfection of wisdom. [Page 523] [Page 524] [Page 525] **The Discourse on the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata** Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, there are four kinds of great compassion belonging to a Tathāgata. What are these four? First, the great compassion of a Tathāgata is immeasurable and boundless; it is not shared by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Second, the great compassion of a Tathāgata is impartial and universal; it does not discriminate between friend and foe. Third, the great compassion of a Tathāgata is constant and uninterrupted; it never ceases throughout the three times. Fourth, the great compassion of a Tathāgata is free from attachment and obstruction; it penetrates all realms of existence without hindrance. Bhikṣus, these are the four kinds of great compassion belonging to a Tathāgata. Because he possesses these four, a Tathāgata is able to deliver all sentient beings from suffering and establish them in the state of ultimate nirvāṇa. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One: "World-Honored One, what is the cause and condition for a Tathāgata to give rise to such great compassion? The Blessed One told Ānanda: "Good son, the Tathāgata’s great compassion arises from the perfection of wisdom. It arises from the cultivation of the four immeasurables. It arises from the realization of the non-arising of all phenomena. It arises from the vision of the equality of all sentient beings. It arises from the vow to liberate all beings without exception. Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva practices the six perfections, he observes that all sentient beings are subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death, yet they do not seek the path to transcend them. Seeing this, he gives rise to great compassion. He observes that sentient beings are bound by the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, yet they do not seek the Dharma to sever them. Seeing this, he gives rise to great compassion. He observes that sentient beings fall into the three evil realms due to their own afflictions, yet they do not seek the means of escape. Seeing this, he gives rise to great compassion. Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that the great compassion of a Tathāgata is inconceivable and incomparable. When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard the Buddha's teaching, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. [Page 524] **The Discourse on the Ten Powers of the Tathāgata** At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, a Tathāgata possesses ten powers. What are these ten? 1. The power of knowing the possible and the impossible. 2. The power of knowing the ripening of karma. 3. The power of knowing various inclinations. 4. The power of knowing various dispositions. 5. The power of knowing the paths leading everywhere. 6. The power of knowing the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and equanimities. 7. The power of knowing the recollection of past lives. 8. The power of knowing the death and rebirth of beings.

9. The power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows. 10. The power of knowing the destruction of all defilements. Because he possesses these ten powers, a Tathāgata is fearless in the great assembly and turns the wheel of the Dharma. [Page 525] **The Discourse on the Four Fearlessnesses** The Blessed One continued: "Bhikṣus, a Tathāgata possesses four fearlessnesses. What are these four? 1. I claim to have attained supreme perfect enlightenment; if anyone in the world should challenge me, saying that I have not realized these dharmas, I see no ground for such a charge. Therefore, I abide in fearlessness. 2. I claim to have exhausted all outflows; if anyone in the world should challenge me, saying that these outflows are not yet exhausted, I see no ground for such a charge. Therefore, I abide in fearlessness. 3. I teach the dharmas that obstruct the path; if anyone in the world should challenge me, saying that these dharmas do not actually constitute obstructions, I see no ground for such a charge. Therefore, I abide in fearlessness. 4. I teach the noble eightfold path leading to the cessation of suffering; if anyone in the world should challenge me, saying that this path cannot lead to the cessation of suffering, I see no ground for such a charge. Therefore, I abide in fearlessness. Possessing these four fearlessnesses, a Tathāgata dwells in peace and security, teaching the Dharma to the four assemblies. When the Buddha had finished speaking, the bhikṣus were filled with joy and received his words with faith. *** **The Discourse on the Three Kinds of Knowledge** The Blessed One further addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, a Tathāgata possesses three kinds of knowledge. What are these three? 1. The knowledge of the past, which knows the causes and conditions of all phenomena without error. 2. The knowledge of the future, which knows the destinations and rebirths of all beings without confusion. 3. The knowledge of the present, which knows the nature of all dharmas as they truly are, free from attachment or aversion. With these three knowledges, a Tathāgata is able to guide sentient beings according to their capacities, leading them to the city of Nirvāṇa. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having heard the Buddha’s words, the bhikṣus were delighted and put them into practice. *** **The Discourse on the Eight Liberations** The Blessed One further addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, a Tathāgata has fully realized the eight liberations. What are these eight? 1. Possessing form, one perceives forms. 2. Not perceiving internal forms, one perceives external forms. 3. With the thought of beauty, one attains liberation. 4. Transcending perceptions of form, one enters the sphere of infinite space. 5. Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness. 6. Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness. 7. Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. 8. Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the cessation of perception and feeling. Having realized these eight liberations, a Tathāgata is able to manifest various miraculous transformations and benefit all sentient beings. When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the great assembly, having heard the profound teaching, bowed in reverence and departed. *** **The Discourse on the Six Supernormal Knowledges** The Blessed One further addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, a Tathāgata possesses six supernormal knowledges. What are these six? 1. The supernormal knowledge of psychic power, which can shake the earth and travel through space. 2. The supernormal knowledge of the divine ear, which hears sounds both celestial and human. 3. The supernormal knowledge of others' minds, which knows the thoughts and intentions of all beings. 4. The supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, which remembers countless kalpas of existence. 5. The supernormal knowledge of the divine eye, which sees the death and rebirth of all beings. 6. The supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, which realizes the end of all suffering. Endowed with these six supernormal knowledges, a Tathāgata acts as a teacher of gods and men, a self-become one, and a peerless guide. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. There, the Blessed One taught this discourse on the qualities of a Tathāgata. All who heard it were inspired and followed his instructions. *** **The Discourse on the Four Reliances** The Blessed One further addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus,

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his profound Prajñāpāramitā, perceives that all five aggregates are empty, and thus he delivers all beings from suffering and distress. Then the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, how does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, perceive that the five aggregates are empty? The Buddha said to the Venerable Śāriputra: “Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind; no form, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touch, no object of mind; no realm of the eye up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajñāpāramitā and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all inverted dreams and delusions, he attains ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra. It is able to remove all suffering and is true and not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. [532] At that time, the entire assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others—having heard what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. [Page 691–693] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive one who courses in the perfection of wisdom. This is because all these phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness. He does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness. He does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness. He does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness. He does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness. He does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness. Why is this? Because all these phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. Moreover, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of giving, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the internal and external. He does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness, nor does he perceive the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the emptiness of the infinite, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of inherent nature, or the emptiness of the nature of non-existence. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness, nor does he perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path. He does not perceive the four meditative concentrations, nor does he perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, or the eight liberations. He does not perceive the nine successive meditative attainments, nor does he perceive the ten totalities, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Why is this? Because all these phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti, it is in this way that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend any phenomenon whatsoever, and thereby trains in the perfection of wisdom.”

[[page 703-to-703]] [[page 704-to-704]] [[page 705-to-705]] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. It should be understood as such. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle’? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, the great vehicle of the Śrāvakas, and the great vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas; because it is the great vehicle that leads to the transcendence of all suffering; because it is the great vehicle that brings about the realization of the unconditioned; because it is the great vehicle that carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra; because it is the great vehicle that establishes one in the city of Nirvāṇa; for these reasons, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard this teaching of the Blessed One, was filled with joy and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how many kinds of Bodhisattvas are there? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there are three kinds of Bodhisattvas: those who have newly set out in the vehicle, those who have practiced for a long time, and those who are irreversible. “Blessed One, what are the characteristics of a Bodhisattva who has newly set out in the vehicle? “Ānanda, a Bodhisattva who has newly set out in the vehicle is characterized by faith, devotion, and the aspiration for enlightenment. He is intent on hearing the Dharma, is diligent in practice, and seeks the company of spiritual friends. However, he is not yet firm in his resolve and may still turn back from the path. “What are the characteristics of a Bodhisattva who has practiced for a long time? “Ānanda, a Bodhisattva who has practiced for a long time possesses deep roots of merit and wisdom. He is skilled in the means of conversion (upāya-kauśalya), is patient with the sufferings of saṃsāra, and does not seek personal liberation alone. He is dedicated to the welfare of all sentient beings and is unwavering in his commitment to the Mahāyāna. “What are the characteristics of an irreversible Bodhisattva? “Ānanda, an irreversible Bodhisattva is one who has attained the stage of non-retrogression. He is incapable of falling back into the states of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. His mind is firmly established in the six perfections, and he possesses the marks of a Buddha. He is able to manifest various forms of existence for the sake of sentient beings, yet remains free from attachment. He is endowed with the power of memory and never forgets the teachings he has received. Such, Ānanda, are the characteristics of an irreversible Bodhisattva. When this teaching was spoken, the Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly were delighted and praised the words of the Blessed One. Thus ends the Exposition of the Great Vehicle, the seventy-third chapter of the Great Vaipulya Sūtra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. [[page 703-to-703]] Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should we honor this Dharma-discourse? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, you should honor this Dharma-discourse as you would honor the Tathāgata himself. For this Dharma-discourse contains the essence of all the Buddhas of the past, present, and future. Whoever upholds this Dharma-discourse, Ānanda, is upholding the lineage of the Buddhas. Whoever recites this Dharma-discourse, Ānanda, is reciting the path to enlightenment. Whoever writes down this Dharma-discourse, Ānanda, is writing down the seeds of Buddhahood. Therefore, Ānanda, you should honor this Dharma-discourse with flowers, incense, banners, and parasols, and you should protect it with all your might. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard these instructions, bowed down at the feet of the Blessed One and departed. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma-discourse? How should it be remembered? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is named ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. It should also be known as ‘The Lamp of Wisdom,’ ‘The Treasury of Merit,’ and ‘The Guide to the City of Nirvāṇa. Remember it thus, Ānanda, and teach it to others. When this teaching was spoken, the Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly were filled with joy and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Thus ends the Exposition of the Great Vehicle, the seventy-fourth chapter of the Great Vaipulya Sūtra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. [[page 704-to-704]] Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how many kinds of obstacles are there to the practice of the Bodhisattvas? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there are five kinds of obstacles to the practice of the Bodhisattvas: the obstacle of external distractions, the obstacle of internal afflictions, the obstacle of wrong views, the obstacle of lack of diligence, and the obstacle of attachment to worldly gain. “Blessed One, what is the obstacle of external distractions? “Ānanda, the obstacle of external distractions refers to being preoccupied with worldly affairs, social gatherings, and idle talk, which prevent one from finding the time to practice the Dharma. “What is the obstacle of internal afflictions? “Ānanda, the obstacle of internal afflictions refers to the arising of greed, hatred, and delusion within the mind, which cloud one’s wisdom and lead to unwholesome actions. “What is the obstacle of wrong views? “Ānanda, the obstacle of wrong views refers to holding onto false doctrines, denying the law of cause and effect, and rejecting the teachings of the Buddhas. “What is the obstacle of lack of diligence? “Ānanda, the obstacle of lack of diligence refers to being lazy, indolent, and lacking the resolve to cultivate the virtues necessary for enlightenment. “What is the obstacle of attachment to worldly gain? “Ānanda, the obstacle of attachment to worldly gain refers to seeking fame, wealth, and honor rather than seeking the true Dharma, which leads one away from the path of liberation. “Ānanda, by avoiding these five obstacles and cultivating their opposites, a Bodhisattva can swiftly attain supreme, perfect enlightenment. When this teaching was spoken, the Venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly were filled with joy and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. [page 709-to-709] [page 710-to-710] [page 711-to-711] **The Chapter on the Non-Self (Anātman)** Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of selflessness. What are these four? Mahāmati, what is the selflessness of persons? It refers to the fact that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are devoid of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, or a human being. Because they are merely a collection of causes and conditions, they are like an illusion or a dream; thus, it is called the selflessness of persons. Next, Mahāmati, what is the selflessness of phenomena? It refers to the fact that all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are devoid of a creator, a doer, or an enjoyer. They arise from the habit-energy of false discrimination (*vikalpa-vāsanā*) and are devoid of intrinsic nature. Thus, it is called the selflessness of phenomena. Next, Mahāmati, what is the selflessness of the characteristics of phenomena? It refers to the fact that the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, as well as the characteristics of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects, are all devoid of self-nature. They are like clouds, lightning, or a mirage, appearing through the power of delusion. Thus, it is called the selflessness of the characteristics of phenomena. Finally, Mahāmati, what is the selflessness of the nature of phenomena? It refers to the fact that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), suchness (*tathatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are all devoid of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). They are not established by words or names, and they transcend the realm of dualistic thought. Thus, it is called the selflessness of the nature of phenomena. If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can thoroughly understand these four kinds of selflessness, he will quickly attain the stage of Buddhahood and be able to transform the habit-energy of false discrimination.

Therefore, Mahāmati, you should practice with diligence. [page 709-to-709] **The Chapter on the Tathāgatagarbha** Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the womb of the Tathāgatas. It is the storehouse of all the Buddhas' teachings. It is neither born nor does it perish; it is eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging. However, because it is covered by the sheaths of the seven consciousnesses, it appears as if it were subject to birth and death. Mahāmati, this Tathāgatagarbha is the same as the *ālayavijñāna*, but its nature is fundamentally pure. It is like a great ocean where waves arise due to the wind of objects, yet the water itself remains unmoved. Because ordinary beings do not understand this, they cling to the notion of a self. The Tathāgata, out of compassion, teaches that the Tathāgatagarbha exists so that they may abandon their fear of selflessness and enter the path of the Great Vehicle. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should know that the Tathāgatagarbha is not the same as the self taught by the non-Buddhist philosophers. It is the ultimate truth, the essence of all dharmas, and the source of all wisdom. You should cultivate this understanding with diligence. Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the destruction of life, abstaining from the destruction of life, laying aside the rod and the sword, modest, merciful, compassionate toward all living beings. He dwells having abandoned taking what is not given, abstaining from taking what is not given, taking only what is given, expecting only what is given, being pure in his hands and clean in his bowl. He dwells having abandoned unchastity, observing celibacy, living apart, refraining from the vulgar practice of sexual intercourse. He dwells having abandoned false speech, abstaining from false speech, a speaker of truth, one established in truth, trustworthy, reliable, no deceiver of the world. He dwells having abandoned divisive speech, abstaining from divisive speech; he does not repeat here what he has heard elsewhere for the purpose of dividing those people from these, nor does he repeat there what he has heard here for the purpose of dividing these people from those; thus he is one who reconciles those who are divided, a promoter of harmony, who delights in concord, who enjoys concord, who speaks words that promote concord. He dwells having abandoned harsh speech, abstaining from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, words that reach the heart, courteous, desired by many, and agreeable to many. He dwells having abandoned idle chatter, abstaining from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the Vinaya; at the right time he speaks such words as are worth recording, reasonable, moderate, and connected with good. He avoids sitting in private with women, girls, eunuchs, men of low birth, or women who have lost their husbands; he does not frequent assemblies, taverns, or gambling houses; he does not associate with outcasts, hunters, fishermen, thieves, or those who follow the profession of executioners. He does not accept gold and silver, raw grain, raw meat, women and girls, male and female slaves, goats and sheep, fowl and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares, fields and lands, or messengers and servants. He does not go on errands or run messages; he does not buy and sell; he does not use false weights, false metals, or false measures; he does not take bribes, deceive, cheat, or act fraudulently. He maintains himself by a livelihood that is blameless and pure. This, monks, is called a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the destruction of life, abstaining from the destruction of life... [as above] ...he maintains himself by a livelihood that is blameless and pure. But he does not encourage others to abandon the destruction of life, to abstain from the destruction of life, to lay aside the rod and the sword, to be modest, merciful, and compassionate toward all living beings. He does not encourage others to abandon taking what is not given... This, monks, is called a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, monks, is one a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the destruction of life, abstaining from the destruction of life... [Page 823–825] **The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Skillful Means** At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas: “O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to enter the gate of skillful means should first cultivate the four immeasurables. What are these four? They are: immeasurable loving-kindness, immeasurable compassion, immeasurable sympathetic joy, and immeasurable equanimity. Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the six perfections. What are these six? They are: the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. Moreover, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. What are these thirty-seven? They are: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. In addition, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should master the ten stages of the bodhisattva. What are these ten? They are:

the stage of joy, the stage of purity, the stage of radiance, the stage of brilliance, the stage of difficult victory, the stage of presence, the stage of far-reaching, the stage of immovability, the stage of good intelligence, and the stage of the cloud of dharma. Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand the two kinds of emptiness. What are these two? They are: the emptiness of phenomena and the emptiness of non-existence. Also, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should realize the three gates of liberation. What are these three? They are: the gate of emptiness, the gate of signlessness, and the gate of wishlessness. Moreover, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should perfect the four unhindered knowledges. What are these four? They are: unimpeded knowledge of meaning, unimpeded knowledge of phenomena, unimpeded knowledge of language, and unimpeded knowledge of eloquence. In addition, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should attain the ten powers of a Tathāgata. What are these ten? They are: the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, the power of knowing the ripening of karma, the power of knowing various inclinations, the power of knowing various dispositions, the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties, the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere, the power of knowing meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and states of equipoise, the power of knowing past lives, the power of knowing death and rebirth, and the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows. Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the four fearlessnesses. What are these four? They are: fearlessness regarding the realization of all-encompassing knowledge, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of all outflows, fearlessness regarding the teaching of the obstacles to the path, and fearlessness regarding the teaching of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Also, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should maintain the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. What are these eighteen? They are: the Buddha does not have erroneous conduct; the Buddha does not have confused speech; the Buddha does not have loss of mindfulness; the Buddha does not have non-equanimity of mind; the Buddha does not have lack of desire to act; the Buddha does not have lack of discernment; the Buddha does not have lack of diligence; the Buddha does not have loss of meditative concentration; the Buddha does not have loss of wisdom; the Buddha does not have loss of liberation; the Buddha does not have loss of the knowledge and vision of liberation; the Buddha’s bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and followed by knowledge; the Buddha’s verbal actions are preceded by knowledge and followed by knowledge; the Buddha’s mental actions are preceded by knowledge and followed by knowledge; the Buddha has no ignorance regarding the past; the Buddha has no ignorance regarding the future; and the Buddha has no ignorance regarding the present. Finally, O sons of the Buddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should aspire to the great vow of universal salvation. This vow is as vast as space and encompasses all sentient beings without exception. By relying on these practices, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly attain supreme, perfect enlightenment. [Page 824] At that time, the venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him: “World-Honored One, what is the cause and condition for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to be called a ‘Great Being’? The Buddha replied to Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to a heart of great compassion, desires to deliver all sentient beings, and practices the path of the six perfections without regressing, he is therefore called a ‘Great Being. Furthermore, Śāriputra, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the wisdom of emptiness and realizes that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature, yet does not abandon the work of saving sentient beings, he is therefore called a ‘Great Being. Also, Śāriputra, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the state of signlessness, yet manifests various forms according to the needs of beings to guide them, he is therefore called a ‘Great Being. Moreover, Śāriputra, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the state of wishlessness, yet generates the great vows of the bodhisattva, he is therefore called a ‘Great Being. [Page 825] Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these skillful means, how should he contemplate the nature of the mind? The Buddha told Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate the mind as being like an illusion, having no real substance. He should contemplate the mind as being like a dream, arising from the conditions of delusion. He should contemplate the mind as being like a reflection, appearing according to the objects before it. He should contemplate the mind as being like an echo, produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions. He should contemplate the mind as being like a mirage, appearing in the heat of the sun but lacking any reality.

He should contemplate the mind as being like a floating bubble, arising and perishing in an instant. He should contemplate the mind as being like a flash of lightning, appearing for a moment and then vanishing. He should contemplate the mind as being like a cloud, gathering and dispersing without permanence. He should contemplate the mind as being like empty space, pervading all places yet devoid of form. Śāriputra, by contemplating the mind in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will transcend all attachments and attain the true nature of all phenomena. Thus spoke the Buddha. Having heard this, the assembly of bodhisattvas and the great disciples were filled with joy and faithfully practiced what they had been taught. [End of Volume]
