Emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. “Therefore, Ānanda, all phenomena are marked by emptiness. They are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness. There is no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, and no mind. There is no sight, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touch, and no object of mind. There is no realm of sight, up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness. There is no ignorance, and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no aging and death, and no extinction of aging and death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path. There is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, the Bodhisattva relies on *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the heart of non-attachment, free from all hindrances. Because there are no hindrances, there is no fear. Having transcended all inverted dreams and thoughts, he attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*. “All Buddhas of the three times, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. When the Buddha had spoken these words, the Venerable Ānanda, as well as the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, the great śrāvakas, and the entire world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. *The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom* (Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra) [page 880-to-880] [page 881-to-881] [page 882-to-882]

[Page 913–915] [Page 913] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent self-nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the perfected self-nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of all phenomena. [Page 914] Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is that which is grasped by the ignorant and simple-minded through names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) regarding objects that have no reality; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the imagined self-nature. What is the dependent self-nature? It is that which arises from the causal conditions of the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination; it is the manifestation of the various forms of consciousness, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, which do not exist as external objects but appear as such due to the mind’s own projection. This is called the dependent self-nature. What is the perfected self-nature? It is the state of the dependent nature being eternally free from the imagined nature; it is the non-duality of subject and object, the absence of increase or decrease, and the realization of the true nature of all things. This is called the perfected self-nature. What is the self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of all phenomena? It is the *tathatā* (suchness), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the signless (*animitta*), and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which serves as the ground for the appearance of all dharmas while remaining unchanging. This is called the self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of all phenomena. [Page 915] Moreover, Mahāmati, the imagined self-nature is characterized by the proliferation of conceptualization (*prapañca*) based on names and signs. The dependent self-nature is characterized by the arising of the eight consciousnesses through the power of causes and conditions. The perfected self-nature is characterized by the cessation of all conceptual proliferation and the realization of the non-arising of all dharmas. The self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of all phenomena is characterized by its being the support for both the defiled and the pure states of existence, yet remaining itself beyond all verbal expression. If one does not understand these four kinds of self-nature, Mahāmati, one will fall into the views of eternalism or nihilism, and will fail to enter the path of the Tathāgata. Therefore, you should cultivate yourself in the discernment of these four self-natures. By doing so, you and other Bodhisattvas will quickly attain the stage of *Tathāgata-kāya* and, having attained mastery over all dharmas, will be able to manifest various bodies according to the inclinations of sentient beings to lead them to liberation. Thus, Mahāmati, you should diligently practice this teaching.

[Page 922–924] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-svabhāva*). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of false discrimination? It is the attachment to names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) as being real entities, based on the habit-energy of beginningless false discrimination. This is called the self-nature of false discrimination. Next, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of dependent origination? It is the manifestation of various objects through the power of habit-energy, appearing like a dream or a magical illusion; it is not established by its own nature but arises in dependence upon causes and conditions. This is called the self-nature of dependent origination. Next, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment? It is the realization that the self-nature of dependent origination is devoid of the characteristics of false discrimination, and that it is the state of non-duality and non-conceptualization. This is called the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. Finally, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the ultimate truth? It is the realm of the Tathāgata, which is free from the four propositions (*cātuṣkoṭika*), transcends all linguistic expression, and is realized only by noble wisdom (*prajñā*). This is called the self-nature of the ultimate truth. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself to abandon the attachment to the self-nature of false discrimination and to realize the self-natures of dependent origination, perfect accomplishment, and the ultimate truth. Thus, Mahāmati, you should practice with diligence. Then, at that time, the Blessed One recited these verses: The self-nature of false discrimination is like a dream or a magical illusion; The self-nature of dependent origination is likewise devoid of intrinsic being. When one realizes that dependent origination is empty of false discrimination, This is known as the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. The realm of the Tathāgatas is free from the four propositions; It is beyond words and cannot be expressed by speech. This is the self-nature of the ultimate truth, Which is to be realized by noble wisdom alone. Thus, Mahāmati, you should understand these four kinds of self-nature. By understanding them, you shall quickly attain the stage of a Buddha. [Page 923–924] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, please explain to me the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattvas. How many kinds of stages are there, and what are their characteristics? The Blessed One replied: "Mahāmati, there are ten stages of the Bodhisattvas. What are these ten? They are: the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the stage of stainlessness (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the stage of radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), the stage of brilliance (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), the stage of difficult victory (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), the stage of presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), the stage of far-reaching (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*), the stage of immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*), the stage of good intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), and the stage of the cloud of dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). These are the ten stages of the Bodhisattvas. "Mahāmati, what are the characteristics of the stage of joy? It is when a Bodhisattva, having attained the insight into the non-arising of all phenomena, gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, and because they have abandoned the two kinds of grasping—grasping at a self and grasping at dharmas—they enter the stream of the Dharma and are no longer subject to retrogression. This is called the characteristic of the stage of joy. "Next, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the stage of stainlessness? It is when a Bodhisattva, having purified the mind and intellect, is free from the stains of the two obstructions—the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—and dwells in the state of non-conceptualization. This is called the characteristic of the stage of stainlessness. "Next, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the stage of radiance? It is when a Bodhisattva, having mastered the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the light of wisdom, illuminates the realms of all Buddhas and attains mastery over the elements.

This is called the characteristic of the stage of radiance. "Next, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the stage of brilliance? It is when a Bodhisattva, having attained the light of the Dharma, is able to burn away the fuel of all afflictions and manifest the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. This is called the characteristic of the stage of brilliance. "Next, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the stage of difficult victory? It is when a Bodhisattva, having overcome the difficulties of all worldly paths and entered the path of the noble ones, is able to conquer all Māras and adversaries. This is called the characteristic of the stage of difficult victory. "Next, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the stage of presence? It is when a Bodhisattva, having reached the point where the path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is present before them, is able to transcend them and enter the path of the Tathāgatas. This is called the characteristic of the stage of presence. "Next, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the stage of far-reaching? It is when a Bodhisattva, having traveled far beyond the reach of ordinary people and even the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, enters the realm of the Tathāgatas and attains mastery over the transformations of birth and death. This is called the characteristic of the stage of far-reaching. "Next, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the stage of immovability? It is when a Bodhisattva, having attained the non-discriminative wisdom, is no longer moved by the winds of conceptual thought and dwells in the state of non-retrogression. This is called the characteristic of the stage of immovability. "Next, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the stage of good intelligence? It is when a Bodhisattva, having perfected the analytical wisdoms (*pratisaṃvid*), is able to teach and transform sentient beings according to their capacities, and their eloquence is inexhaustible.

This is called the characteristic of the stage of good intelligence. "Finally, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the stage of the cloud of dharma? It is when a Bodhisattva, having accumulated a vast store of merit and wisdom, rains down the rain of the Dharma upon all sentient beings, just as a great cloud covers the sky and pours forth rain. This is called the characteristic of the stage of the cloud of dharma. "Mahāmati, these are the ten stages of the Bodhisattvas. By practicing according to these characteristics, a Bodhisattva shall quickly attain the stage of Buddhahood. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having heard this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati and the great assembly were filled with joy and faithfully practiced what the Buddha had taught. [Page 924] At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, you should uphold this discourse on the stages of the Bodhisattvas. From now on, you should teach and spread it to others so that the lineage of the Buddhas may never be interrupted. The Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "I shall do as the Blessed One commands. I will ensure that this teaching is preserved and propagated throughout the world. The Blessed One, having spoken these words, rose from his seat and entered the palace of the Tathāgata. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati and the great assembly, having received the Buddha's instruction, bowed their heads in reverence and departed. [Page 961–963] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is no dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught? Subhūti said: “As I understand the meaning of the Blessed One’s teaching, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has taught. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill this billionfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas; and if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to take up even a single verse from this perfection of wisdom and teach it to others—would the former accumulation of merit be the greater? Subhūti said: “Blessed One, the latter would be the greater. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, the dharma taught by the Tathāgata is inexhaustible; and the dharma taught by the Tathāgata is not exhausted by its being taught. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space-element be exhausted? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “In the same way, Subhūti, the dharma taught by the Tathāgata is inexhaustible; and the dharma taught by the Tathāgata is not exhausted by its being taught. Therefore, Subhūti, the accumulation of merit of a son of good family or a daughter of good family who takes up even a single verse from this perfection of wisdom and teaches it to others is indeed the greater. Then the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should one who has set out on the bodhisattva path train in this perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva should train in the thought that ‘all dharmas are empty. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva trains thus, he does not perceive a self, nor a being, nor a soul, nor a person. He does not perceive form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor formations, nor consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor forms, nor eye-consciousness, nor contact at the eye, nor sensation born of contact at the eye. And so on for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. He does not perceive the elements of earth, water, fire, air, or space. He does not perceive the aggregates, nor the sense-fields, nor the elements. He does not perceive dependent origination, nor the fruits of the holy life, nor even nirvāṇa. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of their own marks. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva trains thus, he does not train in the perfection of giving, nor in the perfection of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom. He does not train in the emptiness of the internal, nor in the emptiness of the external, nor in the emptiness of both, nor in the emptiness of emptiness, nor in the great emptiness, nor in the ultimate emptiness, nor in the conditioned emptiness, nor in the unconditioned emptiness, nor in the infinite emptiness, nor in the beginningless emptiness, nor in the non-dispersal emptiness, nor in the essential nature emptiness, nor in the emptiness of all dharmas, nor in the emptiness of own-marks, nor in the emptiness of non-existence, nor in the emptiness of existence, nor in the emptiness of non-attainability, nor in the emptiness of nature, nor in the emptiness of other-nature, nor in the emptiness of both nature and other-nature. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, all these perfections and emptinesses are themselves empty. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because they are empty that these perfections and emptinesses are not apprehended. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva trains thus, he does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but proceeds toward all-knowledge. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva, training in this way, proceed toward all-knowledge? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva, training in this way, perceives neither the sign of form, nor the sign of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He perceives neither the sign of the eye, nor the sign of forms, nor the sign of eye-consciousness, nor the sign of contact at the eye, nor the sign of sensation born of contact at the eye. And so on for the other sense bases. He perceives neither the sign of the elements, nor the sign of the aggregates, nor the sign of the sense-fields, nor the sign of dependent origination. He perceives neither the sign of the fruits of the holy life, nor the sign of nirvāṇa. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all signs are empty of signs. Therefore, a bodhisattva, training in this way, proceeds toward all-knowledge. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, how does a bodhisattva distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, or between worldly and unworldly dharmas, or between defiled and undefiled dharmas, or between conditioned and unconditioned dharmas? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty, yet a bodhisattva, through skill in means, distinguishes between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, and so forth, up to conditioned and unconditioned dharmas. However, he does not apprehend those dharmas, nor does he apprehend the agent who distinguishes them. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, in emptiness, no distinction can be made. It is by means of this very emptiness that a bodhisattva practices the six perfections and matures beings, purifies the buddha-field, and proceeds toward all-knowledge. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva practices the six perfections and matures beings while all dharmas are empty, will he not be deprived of the fruit of his exertion? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty, yet the bodhisattva does not abandon his vow to liberate beings. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the emptiness of dharmas does not conflict with the vow of the bodhisattva. It is precisely because of this emptiness that the bodhisattva practices the six perfections, matures beings, and purifies the buddha-field. Subhūti, if the bodhisattva did not rely on emptiness, he would fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. But because he relies on emptiness, he does not fall into those levels, but proceeds toward all-knowledge. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva relies on emptiness, does he not become attached to emptiness? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva does not become attached to emptiness. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, emptiness is not an object of attachment. If a bodhisattva becomes attached to emptiness, he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom. But if he does not become attached to emptiness, he is practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, does he see any dharma that is not empty? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not see any dharma that is not empty. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all dharmas are included within emptiness. Therefore, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom sees no dharma outside of emptiness. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are included within emptiness, how does a bodhisattva generate the thought of awakening? [pages 973–975] [page 973] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of imagined characteristics (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom (*tathāgata-āryajñāna-svabhāva*). [page 974] Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of imagined characteristics? It is the attachment to names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) regarding objects that do not exist as such; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the self-nature of imagined characteristics. What is the self-nature of dependent origination? It is the manifestation of various forms based on the causal conditions of ignorance and the like, which are devoid of the nature of external objects. Just as a painter, relying on colors and a canvas, produces various images, so too does the mind, relying on the seeds of habit-energy (*vāsanābīja*), manifest the world of vessels and its inhabitants. This is called the self-nature of dependent origination. What is the self-nature of perfected reality? It is the state where the self-nature of dependent origination is free from the imagined characteristics; it is the non-duality of grasper and grasped, and the realization of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. This is called the self-nature of perfected reality. What is the self-nature of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom? It is the realm of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, which transcends the stages of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, and is realized through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) by means of the noble wisdom of non-conceptualization. This is called the self-nature of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom. [page 975] Moreover, Mahāmati, the self-nature of imagined characteristics is established by the false discrimination of ordinary people.

The self-nature of dependent origination is established by the causal conditions of the mind and mental factors. The self-nature of perfected reality is established by the purification of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and the attainment of the non-discriminative wisdom. The self-nature of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom is established by the mastery over all dharmas and the fulfillment of the great vows. If one can thoroughly understand these four kinds of self-nature, one will not fall into the views of eternalism or nihilism, and will quickly attain the stage of a Bodhisattva. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should practice with diligence to realize this. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Venerable Mahāmati and the assembly of Bodhisattvas and great disciples praised the words of the Buddha. *The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Chapter on the Four Kinds of Self-Nature. [End of pages 973–975]

[Page 1003–1004–1005] [Page 1003] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-svabhāva*). [Page 1004] Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of false discrimination? It refers to the attachment to the characteristics of objects as being real, based on the various manifestations of names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) that arise from the habit-energy of beginningless false discrimination. This is called the self-nature of false discrimination. What is the self-nature of dependent origination? It refers to the manifestation of various phenomena arising from the habit-energy of false discrimination, which, though devoid of external objects, appear as if they were external. This is called the self-nature of dependent origination. What is the self-nature of perfected reality? It refers to the realization that the self-nature of dependent origination is eternally free from the characteristics of false discrimination; it is the state of non-duality and the absence of grasping. This is called the self-nature of perfected reality. What is the self-nature of the ultimate truth? It refers to the Tathāgata-garbha, which is the realm of the noble ones (*āryagocara*), free from the dualistic views of existence and non-existence, and characterized by the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

This is called the self-nature of the ultimate truth. [Page 1005] Moreover, Mahāmati, the self-nature of false discrimination is like a dream, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or a reflection. The self-nature of dependent origination is like a magical illusion (*māyā*). The self-nature of perfected reality is like space. And the self-nature of the ultimate truth is the very nature of Nirvana. If one does not understand these four kinds of self-nature, one will fall into the errors of nihilism or eternalism, and fail to realize the true nature of all phenomena. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should cultivate the wisdom that penetrates these four self-natures in order to transcend all worldly attachments and attain the stage of a Buddha. Thus, the Blessed One spoke this verse: "The four kinds of self-nature are taught To those who enter the path of the Great Vehicle; By understanding them, one abandons the two extremes And swiftly attains the state of Buddhahood. Thus the Blessed One spoke. Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the Venerable Mahāmati and the great assembly were filled with joy and practiced accordingly. Thus ends the [Xth] Chapter on the "Four Kinds of Self-Nature" in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. [Page 1003–1004–1005] (End)

[Page 1072–1074] The Blessed One said this to the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the park of the Licchavis and tell them: ‘Venerable sirs, the Blessed One has arrived at the park of the Licchavis and is staying there. “Yes, Lord,” replied the venerable Ānanda to the Blessed One.
